Three formerly hostile nations now stand together under God's blessing. This foreshadows God's intent — he wants to be God of all nations, turning enemies into one family.
The gospel that tears down the dividing wall.

This vision of "enemies blessed together" is fulfilled in Christ: he "has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility," so that Jews and Gentiles "through him... have access... to the Father" (Ephesians 2:14-18). The gospel is exactly this — bringing former enemies together into God's family — all nations will be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3).
Meditation.

In your heart, is there a certain kind of person — a certain group, a certain "enemy camp," whom you secretly feel God's grace shouldn't reach? This passage challenges that thought: God even calls Egypt and Assyria "my people." Today, can you let God's salvation's vast heart expand your view of "who deserves grace"?

以赛亚书 22:22.verse_text: 我必将 大卫 家的钥匙放在他肩头上。他开，无人能关；他关，无人能开。
beats: 一把权柄的钥匙。
这段针对宫廷总管的预言里，神废去自恃的舍伯那，立忠心的以利亚敬接任。神应许把「大卫家的钥匙」放在他肩头上——钥匙象征管理王家的最高权柄。这不只是一次人事更替，更藏着神对一位终极掌钥者的应许。
「放在他肩头上」。
「放在他肩头上」——权柄如重担，压在肩上，意味着责任与承担，而非单单荣耀。这与九章6节「政权必担在他的肩头上」遥相呼应：真正的权柄不是特权，而是甘愿为百姓担起的责任。
「他开，无人能关」。
「他开，无人能关；他关，无人能开。」这位掌钥者拥有不可推翻的权柄——他所决定的，无人能更改。以利亚敬只是影子；真正配得这绝对权柄的，是那位掌管进出神国之门的君王。
拿着钥匙的基督。
启示录三章7节把这节直接归给基督：祂「拿着大卫的钥匙，开了就没有人能关，关了就没有人能开」。祂掌管救恩与神国的门户；祂为信祂的人开了一道「无人能关」的门。人的权柄会更替，祂的钥匙永远在手。
默想。
你的人生里，有哪些「门」是你拼命想开却开不了、或想关却关不上的——一段关系、一个机会、一道拦阻？这节提醒你：真正掌钥的是基督，「他开，无人能关」。今天，你能否把那扇你无力掌控的门，交给这位掌管一切门户的主？
beats_en: A key of authority.

In this prophecy directed at the palace steward, God removes the self-important Shebna, and installs the faithful Eliakim. God promises to place "the key of the house of David" on his shoulder — the key symbolizes the highest authority to manage the royal household. This is not merely a personnel change, but hides a promise of one ultimate keyholder still to come.
"On his shoulder."

"On his shoulder" — authority is like a burden, pressing on the shoulder, meaning responsibility and bearing, not merely glory. This echoes Isaiah 9:6, "the government shall be upon his shoulder": true authority is not privilege, but responsibility willingly carried for the people.
"He shall open, and none shall shut."

"He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open." This keyholder possesses irreversible authority — what he decides, no one can change. Eliakim was only a shadow; the one truly worthy of this absolute authority is that King who governs the gate of entry into God's kingdom.
Christ, who holds the key.

Revelation 3:7 applies this verse directly to Christ: he "has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens." He governs the gates of salvation and God's kingdom; he has opened a door "that no one can shut" for all who believe in him. Human authority changes hands; his key is always in his own.
Meditation.

In your life, what "doors" are you desperately trying to open but can't, or trying to shut but can't — a relationship, an opportunity, an obstacle? This verse reminds you: Christ is the true keyholder, "he opens, and none can shut." Today, can you hand that door you cannot control over to this Lord who governs every door?

以赛亚书 25:8.verse_text: 他已经吞灭死亡直到永远。主耶和华必擦去各人脸上的眼泪，又除掉普天下他百姓的羞辱，因为这是耶和华说的。
beats: 末世的筵席之歌。
这几章是「以赛亚的启示录」，描绘神最终的得胜。在为万民摆设的丰盛筵席之后，神成就一件人类穷尽古今也无力解决的事：祂要亲手废除那最后、最大的仇敌——死亡。这是全本圣经最早、最明亮的胜过死亡的宣告之一。
「吞灭死亡直到永远」。
「他已经吞灭死亡直到永远。」死亡向来是那吞灭众生的，如今反被神吞灭。注意「直到永远」——这不是暂时的缓解，而是彻底、永久的了结。死亡不是被削弱，而是被消灭，再无回头。
「擦去各人脸上的眼泪」。
「主耶和华必擦去各人脸上的眼泪。」这是何等温柔的一幕：全能的神俯身，亲手为每一个人拭去泪水。祂废除死亡，不是冷冰冰的宣判，而是带着抚慰——祂顾念每一滴因死亡与羞辱而流的泪。
已成与将成。
这应许在基督里既已成就、又将完全成就：祂已借复活「把死废去」（提后一10），并要在再来时使这话完全应验——「不再有死亡，也不再有悲哀、哭号、疼痛」，神要亲自擦去他们一切的眼泪（启二十一4）。
默想。
死亡与失丧所带来的眼泪，是否也曾（或正在）浸湿你的脸？这节应许你一个确定的结局：神必吞灭死亡，亲手擦去你的眼泪。今天，当悲伤袭来，你能否把目光投向那必来的日子——不是逃避眼泪，而是确知有一位要亲手拭去它？
beats_en: A song of the end-time feast.

These chapters are "Isaiah's apocalypse," portraying God's ultimate victory. After a lavish feast laid out for all peoples, God accomplishes something humanity has never been able to resolve across all history: he will, with his own hand, abolish the last, greatest enemy — death. This is one of the earliest, brightest declarations of victory over death in the whole Bible.
"Swallowed up death forever."

"He will swallow up death forever." Death has always been the one that swallows all living things, but now it is swallowed by God instead. Notice "forever" — this is not a temporary reprieve, but a complete, permanent end. Death is not weakened, but destroyed, never to return.
"Wipe away tears from all faces."

"And the LORD GOD will wipe away tears from all faces." What a tender scene: the almighty God stoops down, personally wiping away tears for every person. His abolishing of death is not a cold verdict, but comes with comfort — he cares for every tear shed because of death and disgrace.
Already fulfilled, and yet to be fully fulfilled.

This promise is both already fulfilled in Christ, and yet to be completely fulfilled: he has already "abolished death" through his resurrection (2 Timothy 1:10), and will bring this word to complete fulfillment at his return — "death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore," and God will personally wipe away every tear from their eyes (Revelation 21:4).
Meditation.

Have the tears brought by death and loss also soaked (or are soaking) your face? This verse promises you a certain outcome: God will swallow up death, and personally wipe away your tears. Today, when sorrow strikes, can you set your gaze on that certain day to come — not avoiding the tears, but knowing for certain that there is one who will personally wipe them away?

以赛亚书 28:16.verse_text: 所以，主耶和华如此说： 看哪，我在 锡安 放一块石头作为根基， 是试验过的石头， 是稳固根基，宝贵的房角 石 ； 信靠的人必不着急。
beats: 虚谎盟约的对比。
耶路撒冷的首领自夸与死亡立了约、与阴间结了盟，以为靠政治手腕就能躲过灾祸。神拆穿这虚谎的倚靠，随即摆出唯一真实可靠的根基：「看哪，我在锡安放一块石头作为根基。」人所倚赖的假保障必崩塌，神所立的真根基永长存。
「试验过的石头」。
神所放的，是「试验过的石头，是稳固根基，宝贵的房角石」。房角石定整座建筑的方位与稳固。它「试验过」——经得起考验、绝不动摇。在人心惶惶、四处寻找靠山的时代，神说：真正的稳固，只有一块石头。
「信靠的人必不着急」。
「信靠的人必不着急。」原文有「必不慌乱、必不羞愧」之意。把生命建在这块石头上的人，纵然风浪临到，也不至惊慌失措——因为根基稳固，房子就站立得住。信心带来的，是一种在动荡中不慌的安稳。
房角石就是基督。
彼得与保罗都把这节归给基督（彼前二6；罗九33）：祂是神在锡安所立、经过十字架「试验」的房角石。信靠祂的必不至于羞愧；不信的，祂却成了「绊脚的石头」。人生的根基只有两种——建在祂上面，或建在必崩的虚谎上。
默想。
诚实地问：你此刻的安全感，建在什么上面——存款、健康、人脉、计划？这些都可能像「与死亡立的约」一样靠不住。神说，唯一「试验过、稳固」的根基是那块石头。今天，你的生命是建在基督这房角石上，还是建在会崩塌的沙土上？
beats_en: The contrast with a false covenant.

Jerusalem's leaders boasted of making a covenant with death, an alliance with Sheol, thinking political maneuvering could avoid disaster. God exposes this false reliance, then lays out the one truly reliable foundation: "behold, I am the one who has laid as a foundation in Zion, a stone." The false security man depends on will collapse; the true foundation God has laid stands forever.
"A tested stone."

What God has laid is "a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation." The cornerstone determines the whole building's orientation and stability. It has been "tested" — it withstands scrutiny, never shaken. In an age when hearts are anxious, searching everywhere for support, God says: true stability comes from only one stone.
"Whoever believes will not be in haste."

"Whoever believes will not be in haste." The original carries the sense of "will not panic, will not be put to shame." Whoever builds their life on this stone will not be thrown into panic, even when storms come — because the foundation is stable, the house stands firm. What faith brings is a security that does not panic amid upheaval.
The cornerstone is Christ.

Both Peter and Paul apply this verse to Christ (1 Peter 2:6; Romans 9:33): he is the cornerstone God laid in Zion, "tested" through the cross. Whoever trusts in him will not be put to shame; whoever does not believe, he becomes instead a "stone of stumbling." Life's foundation has only two options — built on him, or built on a false thing bound to collapse.
Meditation.

Ask yourself honestly: what is your sense of security right now built on — savings, health, connections, plans? These could all be as unreliable as "a covenant with death." God says the only "tested, sure" foundation is that stone. Today, is your life built on Christ the cornerstone, or on sand bound to collapse?

以赛亚书 32:1.verse_text: 看哪，必有一王凭公义行政； 必有首领藉公平掌权。
beats: 公义之王的异象。
在一连串审判与祸哉之后，以赛亚忽然展开一幅明亮的图景：「看哪，必有一王凭公义行政，必有首领藉公平掌权。」当时的君王多是自私、失职、带来败坏；先知却望见一位截然不同的王——祂的统治以公义与公平为根基。
「凭公义行政」。
「凭公义行政……藉公平掌权。」这位王的特征不是权势的大小，而是治理的品质：公义与公平。真正的好治理，衡量的标准不是能带来多少繁荣，而是是否伸张公义、护庇弱者。这正是世上一切政权最缺、也最被渴望的。
带来更新的统治。
本章接着描绘这王统治下的光景：眼开耳聪、旷野变良田、公义带来平安与安稳。好的王权不只是维持秩序，更能更新一切——使荒凉之地重现生机。真正公义的掌权，是医治的、是带来兴盛的。
那位真正的王。
这位「凭公义行政」的王，唯基督完全应验。祂来是要以公义审判世界（徒十七31），祂的国「是公义、和平，并圣灵中的喜乐」（罗十四17）。世上的政权终必更替、常令人失望；唯有祂的公义统治，永不败坏、永不落空。
默想。
你是否对这世上的掌权者、对公义的缺失感到失望甚至愤怒？以赛亚把眼光引向那位「凭公义行政」的真王。今天，在为地上的不公祷告的同时，你能否把终极的盼望，放在这位必以公义掌权、永不失职的王身上？
beats_en: The vision of a righteous King.

After a series of judgments and woes, Isaiah suddenly unfolds a bright picture: "behold, a king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule in justice." The kings of that time were mostly selfish, derelict, bringing corruption; but the prophet glimpses an entirely different King — his rule founded on righteousness and justice.
"Reign in righteousness."

"Reign in righteousness... rule in justice." This King's mark is not the size of his power, but the quality of his governance: righteousness and justice. The standard for measuring truly good governance is not how much prosperity it brings, but whether it upholds justice, shelters the weak. This is exactly what every earthly government lacks most, and longs for most.
A rule that brings renewal.

This chapter goes on to describe the scene under this king's rule: eyes opened, ears attentive, the wilderness turned into fertile fields, righteousness bringing peace and security. Good kingship not only maintains order, but renews everything — bringing desolate land back to life. Truly righteous rule heals, and brings prosperity.
That truly righteous King.

This King who "reigns in righteousness" is fully realized only in Christ. He came to judge the world in righteousness (Acts 17:31), and his kingdom "is righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Romans 14:17). Earthly powers eventually change hands, often disappointing; only his righteous reign never fails, never falls through.
Meditation.

Do you feel disappointed, even angry, at the rulers of this world, at the lack of justice? Isaiah directs your gaze to that true King who "reigns in righteousness." Today, while praying for injustice on earth, can you also place your ultimate hope on this King who will surely rule in righteousness, and never be derelict?

以赛亚书 37:14-15.verse_text: 希西家 从使者手里接过书信来，看完了，就上耶和华的殿，将书信在耶和华面前展开。希西家 向耶和华祷告说：
beats: 把恐吓摊在神面前。
亚述王西拿基立大军压境，又送来一封满是亵渎、恐吓的信，扬言犹大的神救不了他们。希西家读完信，做了一个意味深长的动作：他上耶和华的殿，「将书信在耶和华面前展开」。他没有先召开军事会议，而是先把威胁原样摊在神面前。
「展开」的动作。
「将书信在耶和华面前展开」——这是何等真实的祷告图画。希西家不是空谈，而是把那封具体的、字字扎心的恐吓信，一字不漏地摊在神眼前，仿佛说：主啊，你看，他们是这样说你的。真祷告，是把最具体的难处带到神面前。
向神祷告，而非向人商议。
「希西家向耶和华祷告」——在国家存亡的关头，他的第一反应是祷告。恐吓最厉害之处，是叫人心慌意乱、四处求助；希西家却让恐吓把他直接推向神。危机没有击垮他的信心，反倒成了他祷告的祭坛。
垂听的神。
希西家祷告的核心是「求你救我们，好叫天下万国都知道惟有你是耶和华」——他把神的荣耀放在自己的安危之上。神当夜就击杀亚述全军。这位垂听祷告、为自己名的缘故施行拯救的神，正是那应许「你们奉我名求什么，我必成就」的主（约十四13-14）。
默想。
当威胁与坏消息临到，你的第一反应是慌乱地找人商量、反复刷新最坏的设想，还是像希西家那样，先把它「展开在耶和华面前」？今天，有没有一封「恐吓信」——一个诊断、一份账单、一句伤人的话，你需要原样摊在神面前，交给祂？
beats_en: Laying the threat out before God.

The Assyrian king Sennacherib's army pressed in, and sent a letter full of blasphemy and threats, boasting that Judah's God could not save them. Hezekiah, having read the letter, did something meaningful: he went up to the house of the LORD and "spread it before the LORD." He did not first call a war council, but first laid the threat, exactly as it was, before God.
The action of "spreading it out."

"Spread it before the LORD" — what a vivid picture of prayer this is. Hezekiah was not merely speaking in vague terms — he laid that concrete, piercing letter of threats, word for word, before God's eyes, as if to say: Lord, look, this is what they say about you. True prayer brings the most concrete difficulty before God.
Praying to God, not consulting with man.

"And Hezekiah prayed to the LORD" — at the moment of the nation's life-or-death crisis, his first response was to pray. What threats do most effectively is throw a person into panic, seeking help everywhere; but Hezekiah let the threat push him straight toward God instead. The crisis did not crush his faith — instead it became his altar of prayer.
The God who hears.

The core of Hezekiah's prayer was "save us, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD" — he placed God's glory above his own safety. God struck down the entire Assyrian army that very night. This God who hears prayer and saves for his own name's sake is exactly that Lord who promised "whatever you ask in my name, this I will do" (John 14:13-14).
Meditation.

When threats and bad news arrive, is your first response to panic and seek advice from everyone, repeatedly refreshing the worst-case scenario, or, like Hezekiah, to first "spread it before the LORD"? Today, is there a "threatening letter" — a diagnosis, a bill, a hurtful word — that you need to lay exactly as it is before God, and hand over to him?

以赛亚书 40:31.verse_text: 但那等候耶和华的必重新得力。 他们必如鹰展翅上腾； 他们奔跑却不困倦， 行走却不疲乏。
beats: 安慰的高峰。
以赛亚书四十章开启「安慰我的百姓」的新篇。神先宣告自己的浩大——祂用手心量诸水、称山岭、视万民如水桶的一滴。到了本章末了，这位无比浩大的神，把祂的能力转向一件事：加给疲乏软弱之人力量。伟大的神，俯就疲惫的人。
「等候耶和华」的应许。
「但那等候耶和华的必重新得力。」得力的关键是「等候」——不是靠自己咬牙硬撑，而是安静地信靠、仰望、把重量交给神。「等候」不是消极的枯坐，而是把源头从自己转向神的一种主动的信靠。
三重的图画。
「如鹰展翅上腾……奔跑却不困倦，行走却不疲乏。」由高飞到奔跑到行走，图画渐渐落到地面。人生高光时如鹰翱翔固然可贵，但更真实的考验，是在漫长平凡的「行走」中不疲乏。神所赐的力量，正够走过每一段单调的日常。
力量的源头。
疲乏困倦是人的必然，连少年人也要疲乏跌倒（40:30）；唯有那位「永在的神」是不倦怠的力量之源。这力量在基督里向我们敞开——祂说「凡劳苦担重担的，可以到我这里来，我就使你们得安息」（太十一28）。得力之道，是回到祂那里。
默想。
你此刻是疲乏、困倦，甚至觉得撑不下去了吗？这节没有叫你更努力，而是叫你「等候耶和华」——把重量从自己身上卸下，交给那位不倦怠的神。今天，你更需要的，或许不是咬牙再挤出一点力气，而是安静下来，重新仰望祂。
beats_en: The peak of comfort.

Isaiah 40 opens a new chapter of "comfort my people." God first declares his own vastness — he measures the waters in the hollow of his hand, weighs the mountains, regards the nations as a drop from a bucket. By the end of this chapter, this immeasurably vast God turns his power toward one thing: giving strength to the weary and weak. The great God stoops to the exhausted.
The promise of "waiting on the LORD."

"But they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength." The key to renewed strength is "waiting" — not gritting your teeth and forcing through alone, but quietly trusting, looking to, handing the weight over to God. "Waiting" is not passive idleness, but a proactive act of trust, shifting the source from oneself to God.
A threefold picture.

"Mount up with wings like eagles... run and not be weary, walk and not faint." From soaring high, to running, to walking, the picture gradually descends to the ground. Life's peak moments of soaring like an eagle are precious, but the more real test is not growing weary in the long, ordinary "walking." The strength God gives is exactly enough for every stretch of monotonous daily life.
The source of strength.

Weariness and exhaustion are inevitable for man — even the young shall faint and be weary (40:30); only that "everlasting God" is the source of tireless strength. This strength is opened to us in Christ — he says "come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). The way to renewed strength is returning to him.
Meditation.

Are you weary, exhausted right now, even feeling you can't hold on? This verse does not tell you to try harder, but tells you to "wait for the LORD" — lay the weight down from your own shoulders, hand it to that untiring God. Today, what you most need may not be gritting your teeth to squeeze out a bit more strength, but quietly stopping, and looking to him anew.

以赛亚书 45:5.verse_text: 我是耶和华，在我以外并没有别神； 除了我以外再没有 神。 你虽不认识我， 我必给你束腰。
beats: 对波斯王的呼召。
神在此对波斯王古列说话——一个还不认识祂的外邦君王。神要用他释放被掳的以色列。奇妙的是，神反复强调一件事：即便古列「不认识我」，掌管他、使用他的，仍是那位独一的真神。历史的舞台上，唯有一位在真正掌权。
「在我以外并没有别神」。
「我是耶和华，在我以外并没有别神。」这是全章反复敲打的主题。在一个众神林立、偶像遍地的世界里，神斩钉截铁地宣告祂的独一。祂不是众多神明中较大的一位，而是唯一真实存在的神——其余的，尽是虚无。
「你虽不认识我」。
「你虽不认识我，我必给你束腰。」神装备、使用古列，甚至先于古列认识祂。这揭示一个惊人的真理：神的主权不受限于人是否认识祂；祂能使不信的君王，也成为成就祂旨意的器皿。整个历史，都在祂的手中运行。
独一的主与救主。
这位独一真神宣告「除我以外，再没有救主」（45:21），并邀万邦「都当仰望我，就必得救」。这独一性在基督里聚焦成救恩的唯一——「除他以外，别无拯救；……没有赐下别的名，我们可以靠着得救」（徒四12）。
默想。
你是否也悄悄在神以外，倚靠着别的「小神」——金钱、地位、掌控感，把安全感分散押注？神说「在我以外并没有别神」。今天，你能否重新认定祂的独一：不只是「诸多倚靠之一」，而是你生命中唯一真实、唯一当仰望的主？
beats_en: A call to the Persian king.

Here God speaks to Cyrus, king of Persia — a Gentile ruler who did not yet know him. God would use him to release the exiled Israelites. Astonishingly, God repeatedly emphasizes one thing: even though Cyrus "does not know me," the one governing him, using him, is still that one true God. On the stage of history, only one is truly in control.
"There is no other God besides me."

"I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God." This theme is hammered home repeatedly throughout the chapter. In a world crowded with gods, idols everywhere, God declares his uniqueness with utter certainty. He is not the greater one among many gods, but the only truly existing God — all the rest are nothing.
"Though you do not know me."

"Though you do not know me, I equip you." God equips and uses Cyrus, even before Cyrus knows him. This reveals an astonishing truth: God's sovereignty is not limited by whether people know him; he can even make an unbelieving king a vessel for accomplishing his will. All of history moves within his hand.
The one Lord and Savior.

This one true God declares "besides me there is no savior" (45:21), and invites all nations to "turn to me and be saved." This oneness is focused, in Christ, into salvation's sole way — "there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4:12).
Meditation.

Are you also secretly relying on other "small gods" besides God — money, status, a sense of control — spreading your security across multiple bets? God says "there is no other God besides me." Today, can you reaffirm his uniqueness anew: not just "one reliance among many," but the one true, one only Lord to look to in your life?

以赛亚书 53:5.verse_text: 哪知他为我们的过犯受害， 为我们的罪孽压伤。 因他受的刑罚，我们得平安； 因他受的鞭伤，我们得医治。
beats: 受苦仆人之歌的心脏。
以赛亚五十三章，是旧约中对基督救赎最清晰、最震撼的预言，写于其成就的七百年前。第五节是这首「受苦仆人之歌」的心脏，用四个短句，把福音的核心——代替受罚——说得淋漓尽致。这里没有一个多余的字，字字都是我们的得赎。
「为我们」的代替。
「他为我们的过犯受害，为我们的罪孽压伤。」两次「为我们」，点出十字架的本质：这是代替。仆人所受的害与压伤，本不该临到祂——那是我们的过犯、我们的罪孽当受的。祂站到了我们的位置上，承担了本属我们的刑罚。
刑罚与鞭伤的交换。
「因他受的刑罚，我们得平安；因他受的鞭伤，我们得医治。」这是一场惊人的交换：祂受刑罚，我们得平安；祂受鞭伤，我们得医治。我们与神之间的和好、我们灵魂最深的创伤的医治，全建立在祂所承受的痛楚之上。
数算这交换。
彼得直接引用这节，指向基督：祂「被挂在木头上，亲身担当了我们的罪……因他受的鞭伤，你们便得了医治」（彼前二24）。每一个「为我们」都是白白的恩典——不是我们配得，而是祂甘愿承担。这是基督徒信仰的根基。
默想。
慢慢再读一遍这节，把每一个「我们」换成「我」：他为「我」的过犯受害，因他受的鞭伤，「我」得医治。你今天最深的愧疚、最需要的平安、最难愈的创伤，基督都已在十字架上为你担当。你是否真的领受了这场「交换」？
beats_en: The heart of the Suffering Servant song.

Isaiah 53 is the Old Testament's clearest, most striking prophecy of Christ's redemption, written seven hundred years before its fulfillment. Verse 5 is the heart of this "Suffering Servant Song," using four short phrases to state, in full, the core of the gospel — substitutionary punishment. Not a single unnecessary word here — every word is our redemption.
The substitution "for us."

"He was wounded for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities." Two "for us" phrases point out the essence of the cross: this is substitution. The wound and the crushing the Servant suffered should never have come upon him — that belonged to our transgressions, our iniquities. He stood in our place, bearing the punishment that was rightfully ours.
The exchange of punishment for wounds.

"Upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed." This is an astonishing exchange: he bore the chastisement, we get peace; he bore the wounds, we get healing. Our reconciliation with God, and the healing of the deepest wound of our souls, are entirely built on the pain he bore.
Counting up this exchange.

Peter directly quotes this verse, pointing to Christ: he "bore our sins in his body on the tree... by his wounds you have been healed" (1 Peter 2:24). Every "for us" is free grace — not because we deserve it, but because he was willing to bear it. This is the foundation of the Christian faith.
Meditation.

Read this verse again slowly, replacing each "we" with "me": he was wounded for "my" transgressions, by his wounds "I" am healed. Your deepest guilt today, your greatest need for peace, your hardest-to-heal wound — Christ has already borne it for you on the cross. Have you truly received this exchange?

以赛亚书 55:8-9.verse_text: 耶和华说：我的意念非同你们的意念； 我的道路非同你们的道路。天怎样高过地， 照样，我的道路高过你们的道路； 我的意念高过你们的意念。
beats: 白白赦免的邀请。
五十五章是一封敞开的邀请：无钱的可以白白来买酒奶，恶人可以离弃己路、归向必广行赦免的神。就在这慷慨得近乎不可思议的赦免之后，神解释祂为何能如此赦免——因为祂的意念与道路，远高过人的。
「非同你们的意念」。
「我的意念非同你们的意念，我的道路非同你们的道路。」人的本能是斤斤计较、恩怨相报，觉得罪该受罚、恩当偿还。神却「广行赦免」。祂能如此白白施恩，正因祂的心思与人根本不在同一个高度。
「天怎样高过地」。
「天怎样高过地，照样，我的道路高过你们的道路。」这不是说神高深莫测、叫人绝望，而是就着上文的赦免说的：祂赦免的深广，高过人所能想象——正如天高过地。人以为罪无可赦之处，正是神恩典最显浩大之处。
高过人心的恩典。
这「高过」的意念与道路，在十字架上显为极致：神竟差爱子替罪人受死，「惟有基督在我们还作罪人的时候为我们死」（罗五8）——这是任何人的逻辑都算不出来的恩典。神的道路高过我们，最动人之处，正在于祂的赦免远超我们所配、所想。
默想。
你是否常用人的逻辑限制神——觉得自己罪太重不配被赦，或觉得某人太可恶不该被神接纳？神说，祂的意念高过你的，如天高过地。今天，你能否放下那把「人的尺」，来领受、也去传扬这份「高过」你一切算计的赦免之恩？
beats_en: An invitation to free forgiveness.

Chapter 55 is an open invitation: those without money may come freely to buy wine and milk, the wicked may forsake their own way and turn to the God who will abundantly pardon. Right after this almost unbelievably generous forgiveness, God explains why he can forgive this way — because his thoughts and ways are far higher than man's.
"Not your thoughts."

"My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways." Man's instinct is to keep score, repay grievance for grievance, feeling that sin deserves punishment and grace must be earned back. But God "will abundantly pardon." He can extend grace so freely exactly because his mind is not on the same level as man's at all.
"As the heavens are higher than the earth."

"As the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways." This is not saying God is unfathomable to the point of despair, but speaks in context of the forgiveness above: the depth and breadth of his forgiveness exceeds what man can imagine — just as the heavens are higher than the earth. Where man thinks sin cannot be forgiven is exactly where God's grace shows itself most vast.
Grace higher than the human heart.

This "higher" thought and way was displayed to its utmost on the cross: God actually sent his beloved Son to die in the sinner's place — "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8) — grace that no human logic could ever calculate. What's most moving about God's ways being higher than ours is exactly that his forgiveness far exceeds what we deserve, what we could imagine.
Meditation.

Do you often limit God with human logic — feeling your own sin too heavy to deserve forgiveness, or feeling someone else too detestable for God to accept? God says his thoughts are higher than yours, as the heavens are higher than the earth. Today, can you lay down that "human ruler," and receive, and also proclaim, this grace of forgiveness that is "higher" than all your calculations?

以赛亚书 61:1.verse_text: 主耶和华的灵在我身上； 因为耶和华用膏膏我， 叫我传好信息给谦卑的人 ， 差遣我医好伤心的人， 报告被掳的得释放， 被囚的出 监牢 ；
beats: 受膏者的宣言。
六十一章开篇，是一位受膏者的自我宣告：神的灵在他身上，差他去传福音、医伤心、报自由。这不是泛泛的使命描述，而是弥赛亚亲自登场的宣言——祂被圣灵膏抹，专为一群特定的人而来：谦卑的、伤心的、被掳的、被囚的。
「传好信息给谦卑的人」。
「传好信息给谦卑的人。」福音的对象，是「谦卑的」——原文也指困苦、卑微、一无所有的人。神的好消息不是给自觉富足、自以为义的人，而是给那些穷乏、知道自己需要恩典的人。承认自己的贫乏，正是领受福音的门。
医治、释放、自由。
「医好伤心的人，报告被掳的得释放，被囚的出监牢。」受膏者带来的，是全方位的释放：情感的医治、身心的自由、被辖制之人的出监。祂来不是要加给人重担、条件，而是要打开一切捆锁,使受压制的得着真自由。
「今天应验了」。
路加福音四章，主耶稣在拿撒勒会堂读的正是这段经文，读完宣告：「今天这经应验在你们耳中了」（路四21）。祂就是那位受膏者；祂的整个事工——医病、赶鬼、赦罪、释放——都是这宣言的兑现。福音的好消息，在祂身上成了活的现实。
默想。
这福音是给「谦卑的、伤心的、被掳的、被囚的」——你是否肯承认，自己正是这样一个需要祂的人？还是你仍靠自己的富足与体面，把自己排除在这好消息之外？今天，在哪一处捆锁里，你需要重新领受这位受膏者带来的释放与自由？
beats_en: The declaration of the anointed one.

Chapter 61 opens with the self-declaration of an anointed one: the Spirit of God is upon him, sending him to preach the gospel, heal the brokenhearted, proclaim freedom. This is not a vague description of a mission, but the personal announcement of the Messiah's arrival — anointed by the Spirit, coming specifically for a particular group of people: the poor, the brokenhearted, the captives, the imprisoned.
"Good news to the poor."

"Good news to the poor." The gospel's audience is "the poor" — the original also refers to the afflicted, the lowly, those with nothing. God's good news is not for those who feel themselves rich, self-righteous, but for those who are needy, who know they need grace. Acknowledging one's own poverty is exactly the door to receiving the gospel.
Healing, release, freedom.

"To bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound." What this anointed one brings is comprehensive release: emotional healing, freedom of body and mind, release for those under bondage. He did not come to add burdens, conditions, but to open every chain, setting the oppressed truly free.
"Today this is fulfilled."

In Luke 4, the Lord Jesus, in the synagogue at Nazareth, read exactly this passage, and after finishing, declared: "today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing" (Luke 4:21). He is that anointed one; his entire ministry — healing, casting out demons, forgiving sins, releasing — was the fulfillment of this declaration. The gospel's good news became living reality in him.
Meditation.

This gospel is for the "poor, brokenhearted, captive, imprisoned" — are you willing to acknowledge you are exactly this kind of person who needs him? Or are you still relying on your own wealth and dignity, excluding yourself from this good news? Today, in what bondage do you need to receive afresh the release and freedom this anointed one brings?

以赛亚书 64:6.verse_text: 我们都像不洁净的人； 所有的义都像污秽的衣服。 我们都像叶子渐渐枯干； 我们的罪孽好像风把我们吹去。
beats: 认罪的祷告。
以赛亚书临近结尾，先知代表百姓向神发出一段深沉的认罪祷告。他不为自己辩护，反而把全民放在神圣洁的光中审视——结果是彻底的破产：连他们最引以为傲的「义」，在神面前也站立不住。这是灵魂真正看见神之后的必然反应。
「义」像污秽的衣服。
「所有的义都像污秽的衣服。」注意——不是说他们的「罪」，而是他们的「义」，那些自以为讨神喜悦的善行。原文的「污秽」指极不洁之物。人靠自己积攒的功德，在圣洁的神面前，非但不能遮羞，反成了需要被洗净的污秽。
枯干与被吹去。
「我们都像叶子渐渐枯干；我们的罪孽好像风把我们吹去。」这是一幅无力自救的图画：人像秋天的枯叶，被罪的风卷走，毫无抵抗之力。先知看清：问题不是做得不够好，而是人从根本上已经枯死、无法自救。
唯靠外来的义。
既然连「义」都是污秽，人就绝无可能靠自己得救——唯一的出路是一件从外面赐下的义。这正指向福音：神「使那无罪的替我们成为罪，好叫我们在他里面成为神的义」（林后五21）。我们所穿的，是基督的义袍，不是自己的破衣。
默想。
你是否也暗暗靠自己的「好行为」在神面前争取地位——觉得做得够多，就够体面了？这节经文戳破这幻想：连你最好的义，也需要被洗净。今天，你能否卸下那件自义的「污秽衣服」，重新披上基督白白赐下的义袍？
beats_en: A prayer of confession.

Nearing the end of Isaiah, the prophet, on behalf of the people, offers a deep prayer of confession before God. He does not defend himself; instead he places the whole nation under God's holy light for examination — the result is total bankruptcy: even their most prided-in "righteousness" cannot stand before God. This is the inevitable response after a soul has truly seen God.
"Righteousness" like filthy rags.

"All our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment." Notice — this speaks not of their "sin," but of their "righteousness," the good deeds they thought pleased God. The original word for "polluted" refers to something extremely unclean. Merit accumulated by one's own effort, before the holy God, not only cannot cover shame — it becomes filth needing to be washed.
Withering and blown away.

"We all fade like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away." This is a picture of utter powerlessness to save oneself: man is like an autumn leaf, swept away by the wind of sin, with no power to resist. The prophet sees clearly: the problem is not doing insufficiently well — man has, at the root, already withered dead, unable to save himself.
Only an imported righteousness.

Since even "righteousness" is filthy, man has absolutely no possibility of saving himself — the only way out is a righteousness given from outside. This points exactly to the gospel: God "made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21). What we wear is the robe of Christ's righteousness, not our own tattered garment.
Meditation.

Are you also secretly relying on your own "good behavior" to strive for standing before God — feeling that if you do enough, you'll be respectable enough? This verse punctures that illusion: even your very best righteousness needs to be washed. Today, are you willing to lay down that "polluted garment" of self-righteousness, and put on afresh the robe of righteousness Christ freely gives?

耶利米书 2:13.verse_text: 因为我的百姓做了两件恶事， 就是离弃我这活水的泉源， 为自己凿出池子， 是破裂不能存水的池子。
beats: 两件恶事。
耶利米一开口传讲神的控诉，就把百姓的罪浓缩成「两件恶事」。这不是罗列一长串违规清单，而是直指罪的根本结构：先是离弃真正的源头，再是转向虚假的替代品。一切偶像崇拜，都是这两步。
离弃活水的泉源。
「离弃我这活水的泉源。」神把自己形容为一口永不干涸、涌流不息的活泉。人最大的悲剧，不是道德上做错了什么，而是转身背离了那唯一能真正解渴的源头。罪的本质，是弃绝神本身。
凿破裂的池子。
「为自己凿出池子，是破裂不能存水的池子。」离开活泉的人不会停止口渴，只会转去自己凿水池——费尽力气自制的替代满足。可这些池子都是「破裂」的，存不住水。人靠自己造的一切满足，最终都会漏光、令人失望。
活水的应许。
耶利米所指的「活水泉源」，在基督里向我们敞开：祂对撒玛利亚妇人说，祂所赐的水要「成为泉源，直涌到永生」（约四14）；又说「人若渴了，可以到我这里来喝」（约七37）。真正的满足，只在回到源头时才寻得着。
默想。
诚实地问：你在为自己凿哪些「破裂的池子」——用什么来填补心里的渴（成就、关系、娱乐、掌控）？它们是否总是漏水、总留下更深的空？今天，你愿不愿意离开这些池子，回到那位「活水的泉源」面前来解渴？
beats_en: Two evils.

The moment Jeremiah begins proclaiming God's indictment, he condenses the people's sin into "two evils." This is not a long list of violations, but points straight to the fundamental structure of sin: first forsaking the true source, then turning to a false substitute. All idolatry is these two steps.
Forsaking the fountain of living waters.

"They have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters." God describes himself as a spring that never dries, ever flowing. Man's greatest tragedy is not some moral wrongdoing, but turning away from the one source that can truly quench thirst. The essence of sin is rejecting God himself.
Hewing broken cisterns.

"And hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water." Those who leave the living spring do not stop being thirsty — they only turn to dig their own cisterns, exhausting themselves to construct a substitute satisfaction. But these cisterns are all "broken," unable to hold water. Every satisfaction man builds for himself eventually leaks dry, leaving disappointment.
The promise of living water.

This "fountain of living waters" Jeremiah speaks of is now open to us in Christ: he told the Samaritan woman that the water he gives "will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life" (John 4:14); and said "if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink" (John 7:37). True satisfaction is found only in returning to the source.
Meditation.

Ask yourself honestly: what "broken cisterns" are you digging for yourself — what are you using to fill the thirst in your heart (achievement, relationships, entertainment, control)? Do they always leak, always leave a deeper emptiness? Today, are you willing to leave these cisterns, and come back before that "fountain of living waters" to quench your thirst?

耶利米书 6:16.verse_text: 耶和华如此说： 你们当站在路上察看， 访问古道， 哪是善道，便行在其间； 这样，你们心里必得安息。 他们却说：我们不行 在其间 。
beats: 站在岔路口的呼召。
在毁灭的预言中间，神发出一个温柔的邀请。祂把百姓比作走到岔路口的旅人，吩咐他们停下来、看清方向：「你们当站在路上察看。」在一个人人急着往前冲的时代，神先叫祂的百姓停步、省察脚下的路。
「访问古道」。
「访问古道，哪是善道，便行在其间。」神指的「古道」，不是怀旧，而是回到起初祂所立的、经得起时间考验的正路——祂的话与祂的约。当新潮的路都通向毁灭时，真正的智慧是回到那条古老而可靠的善道上。
安息的应许。
「这样，你们心里必得安息。」行在神的古道上，结果是「安息」——一种灵魂深处的安稳。这不是靠环境顺遂得来的，而是走在对的路上、与神同行才有的平安。偏离正路的人，得着的只有不安。
「我们不行在其间」。
然而百姓的回应令人心碎：「我们却说：我们不行在其间。」神指明了善道、应许了安息，他们却公然拒绝。这正预表那位站在耶路撒冷城前哭泣的主——祂愿聚拢他们，「只是你们不愿意」（太二十三37）。安息一直敞开，人却常常掉头不顾。
默想。
你是否也活在一种不肯停步的忙乱里，从未真正「站在路上察看」自己走的是什么路？神应许，走在祂的古道上必得安息。今天，你愿不愿意停下来省察——你现在这条路，通向安息，还是通向不安？
beats_en: A call at the crossroads.

In the midst of prophecies of destruction, God issues a tender invitation. He compares the people to a traveler arriving at a fork in the road, telling them to stop and see the way clearly: "stand at the crossroads, and look." In an age when everyone rushes forward, God first tells his people to stop, and examine the road beneath their feet.
"Ask for the ancient paths."

"Ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is, and walk in it." The "ancient paths" God points to are not nostalgia, but returning to the road he originally laid, tested by time — his word and his covenant. When all the trendy roads lead to destruction, true wisdom is returning to that ancient, reliable good way.
The promise of rest.

"And find rest for your souls." Walking on God's ancient path results in "rest" — a security deep in the soul. This does not come from smooth circumstances, but from walking the right road, walking with God. Those who stray from the true path find only unrest.
"We will not walk in it."

Yet the people's response is heartbreaking: "but they said, we will not walk in it." God pointed out the good way, promised rest, yet they openly refused. This foreshadows exactly that Lord who stood weeping before the city of Jerusalem — he longed to gather them, "but you were not willing" (Matthew 23:37). Rest has always stood open, yet man often turns away, unwilling.
Meditation.

Are you also living in a busyness that refuses to stop, never truly having "stood at the crossroads" to examine what road you're walking? God promises: walking his ancient path brings rest. Today, are you willing to stop and examine — does this road you're on now lead to rest, or to unrest?

耶利米书 9:1.verse_text: 但愿我的头为水， 我的眼为泪的泉源， 我好为我百姓 中被杀的人昼夜哭泣。
beats: 流泪的先知。
耶利米素有「流泪的先知」之称，这一节正是缘由。面对百姓的顽梗与将临的毁灭，他没有冷眼旁观、幸灾乐祸，反而心如刀割：「但愿我的头为水，我的眼为泪的泉源。」传讲审判的人，心里却装满了对被审判者的疼痛。
泪水的泉源。
「我的眼为泪的泉源，我好为我百姓中被杀的人昼夜哭泣。」耶利米恨不得自己整个人化成泪泉，日夜为百姓哀哭。真正属神的心肠，不是站在道德高地上指责罪人，而是为罪人的沉沦流泪、代求、同悲。
与神同哀。
耶利米的眼泪，其实映照着神自己的心。神宣告审判，却「不喜悦恶人死亡」（结三十三11）。先知的哀哭，让我们瞥见审判背后那颗破碎的父心——祂管教，却从不冷酷；祂降罚，心里却在痛。
为耶路撒冷哭泣的主。
耶利米的眼泪，在基督身上得着完全——祂望着耶路撒冷放声痛哭（路十九41），又在拉撒路墓前流泪（约十一35）。祂不是远远宣判世人的神，而是道成肉身、进到我们的悲哀中、亲自为我们流泪的救主。
默想。
面对身边人的悖逆或沉沦，你的第一反应是批评论断，还是像耶利米那样心里疼痛、为他们流泪代求？神的心肠，是为失丧者哀哭的心肠。今天，有没有一个人，神要你不再指责，而是为他流一滴真诚的泪、献上一句真切的祷告？
beats_en: The weeping prophet.

Jeremiah has long been called "the weeping prophet," and this verse is exactly why. Facing the people's stubbornness and the coming destruction, he does not look on with cold indifference or gloat — instead his heart is torn: "oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears." The one proclaiming judgment carries a heart full of pain for those being judged.
A fountain of tears.

"And my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people." Jeremiah wishes his whole self could become a fountain of tears, weeping for the people day and night. A truly godly heart does not stand on moral high ground condemning sinners, but weeps, intercedes, and grieves alongside sinners in their ruin.
Grieving together with God.

Jeremiah's tears, in fact, reflect God's own heart. God declares judgment, yet "has no pleasure in the death of the wicked" (Ezekiel 33:11). The prophet's grief lets us glimpse the broken father's heart behind the judgment — he disciplines, yet is never cold; he brings punishment, yet his heart aches.
The Lord who wept over Jerusalem.

Jeremiah's tears found complete fulfillment in Christ — he wept aloud looking at Jerusalem (Luke 19:41), and wept at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:35). He is not a distant God pronouncing judgment on the world, but a Savior who became flesh, entered our grief, and personally wept for us.
Meditation.

Facing the rebellion or ruin of those around you, is your first response criticism and judgment, or, like Jeremiah, an aching heart, weeping and interceding for them? God's heart is a heart that grieves for the lost. Today, is there someone God wants you to stop criticizing, and instead shed a genuine tear for, offering a sincere prayer?

耶利米书 18:6.verse_text: 「耶和华说： 以色列 家啊，我待你们，岂不能照这窑匠弄泥吗？ 以色列 家啊，泥在窑匠的手中怎样，你们在我的手中也怎样。
beats: 窑匠家的功课。
神差耶利米下到窑匠的家，看他做工。窑匠手中的器皿做坏了，他就把泥重新揉过、另作一个。神借这日常的一幕，向以色列说出一个关于祂主权的深刻真理：造物者对祂手中的泥，拥有完全的权柄。
「泥在窑匠的手中」。
「泥在窑匠的手中怎样，你们在我的手中也怎样。」这不是要贬低人，而是要校正人的位置：我们是被造的泥，神是塑造的匠。泥无法指挥窑匠，也无法自我成形。承认「我在祂手中」，是一切谦卑与信靠的起点。
主权中的怜悯。
值得注意的是，窑匠见器皿做坏了，不是丢弃，而是「重作」。神的主权不是冷酷的专断，而是带着重塑的怜悯：祂有权、也有意，把破损的生命重新揉过、再造成合用的器皿。审判的话语里，藏着重造的恩典。
被重塑的器皿。
保罗也用「窑匠与泥」讲神的主权与拣选（罗九20-21）。而这位窑匠最终不是要毁弃我们，而是要使我们「模成他儿子的模样」（罗八29）。在基督里，破损的泥被重新塑造，成为「贵重的器皿……合乎主用」（提后二21）。
默想。
你是否常想挣脱神的手、按自己的意思「自我成形」，一旦生命被祂重新揉捏就抗拒不安？这节提醒你：你是泥，祂是窑匠——而且是满有怜悯、要把你重造为美器的窑匠。今天，你能否安息在祂手中，让祂随己意塑造你？
beats_en: The lesson at the potter's house.

God sent Jeremiah down to the potter's house, to watch him work. When the vessel in the potter's hand was spoiled, he reworked the clay, making it into another vessel. God, through this everyday scene, spoke to Israel a profound truth about his sovereignty: the Creator has complete authority over the clay in his hand.
"As the clay is in the potter's hand."

"As the clay is in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand." This is not meant to demean man, but to correct man's position: we are the created clay, God is the shaping potter. Clay cannot direct the potter, nor form itself. Acknowledging "I am in his hand" is the starting point of all humility and trust.
Mercy within sovereignty.

It's worth noting that when the potter sees the vessel spoiled, he does not throw it away, but "reworks" it. God's sovereignty is not cold arbitrariness, but comes with reshaping mercy: he has both the right and the intent to knead a broken life back together, remaking it into a usable vessel. Within the words of judgment lies the grace of remaking.
The reshaped vessel.

Paul also uses "the potter and the clay" to speak of God's sovereignty and election (Romans 9:20-21). And this potter's ultimate intent is not to destroy us, but to make us "conformed to the image of his Son" (Romans 8:29). In Christ, the broken clay is reshaped, becoming "a vessel for honorable use... useful to the master" (2 Timothy 2:21).
Meditation.

Do you often want to wrench yourself free from God's hand, "self-form" according to your own will, resisting uneasily whenever your life is reworked by him? This verse reminds you: you are the clay, he is the potter — and a potter full of mercy, wanting to remake you into a fine vessel. Today, can you rest in his hand, and let him shape you as he wills?

耶利米书 20:9.verse_text: 我若说：我不再提耶和华， 也不再奉他的名讲论， 我便心里觉得 似乎有烧着的火闭塞在我骨中， 我就含忍不住，不能自禁。
beats: 先知的挣扎。
这一段是耶利米最赤裸的内心独白。传神的话给他带来的，只有讥笑、逼迫与羞辱。他一度想放弃：「我不再提耶和华，也不再奉他的名讲论。」连神的仆人，也会走到心力交瘁、想撂挑子的边缘。
骨中烧着的火。
然而他做不到：「我便心里觉得似乎有烧着的火闭塞在我骨中，我就含忍不住，不能自禁。」神的话在他里面像火，压不住、藏不了。真正被神话语抓住的人，即使受尽逼迫想放弃，那话仍在里面燃烧，逼他不得不说。
真实的软弱与忠心。
耶利米没有假装刚强。他的忠心不是没有挣扎的忠心，而是在极度想放弃之中，仍被神的话托住、无法真正离开的忠心。圣经如实记下他的软弱，正让每个疲惫的事奉者知道：挣扎不等于失败。
不能不说的福音。
耶利米骨中的火，在使徒身上再次燃起——保罗说「我不传福音就有祸了」（林前九16），彼得约翰说「我们所看见所听见的，不能不说」（徒四20）。当基督的爱真正激励一个人，福音就成了骨中压不住的火。
默想。
在服事或为主发声的路上，你是否也曾因灰心、逼迫或无人回应而想「不再提耶和华」？耶利米的经历告诉你：软弱与挣扎是真实的，但神的话若真在你里面，它会像火一样重新燃起。今天，是什么在浇熄那火——你需要重新回到神的话前吗？
beats_en: The prophet's struggle.

This passage is Jeremiah's rawest inner monologue. Proclaiming God's word brought him nothing but mockery, persecution, and shame. At one point he wanted to give up: "I will not mention him, or speak any more in his name." Even God's servant can reach the edge of exhaustion, wanting to throw in the towel.
Fire burning in his bones.

Yet he couldn't: "there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot." God's word within him was like fire, uncontainable, unhideable. A person truly gripped by God's word, even amid persecution, wanting to give up, still has that word burning within, forcing them to speak.
Real weakness and real faithfulness.

Jeremiah did not pretend to be strong. His faithfulness was not faithfulness without struggle, but faithfulness that, even in extreme desire to give up, was still upheld by God's word, unable to truly leave. Scripture faithfully records his weakness, letting every weary servant know: struggling is not the same as failing.
A gospel that cannot be left unsaid.

The fire in Jeremiah's bones burned again in the apostles — Paul said "woe to me if I do not preach the gospel" (1 Corinthians 9:16), Peter and John said "we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard" (Acts 4:20). When Christ's love truly moves a person, the gospel becomes a fire in the bones that cannot be suppressed.
Meditation.

On the road of serving or speaking for the Lord, have you ever, out of discouragement, persecution, or lack of response, wanted to "no longer mention the LORD"? Jeremiah's experience tells you: weakness and struggle are real, but if God's word is truly within you, it will burn again like fire. Today, what is quenching that fire — do you need to return to God's word afresh?

耶利米书 23:6.verse_text: 在他的日子， 犹大 必得救， 以色列 也安然居住。他的名必称为『耶和华－我们的义』。」
beats: 昏君之后的应许。
耶利米刚痛斥了那些「使羊群四散」的坏牧人（犹大历代失职的君王），随即神应许要亲自兴起一位「公义的苗裔」——真正的大卫子孙。在一片王朝败落的黑暗里，神点亮了弥赛亚的盼望。
「犹大必得救」。
「在他的日子，犹大必得救，以色列也安然居住。」失职的君王只带来分裂与掳掠；这位公义之王一来，就带来拯救与安稳。真正的君王，衡量的不是权势，而是他能否使百姓得救、得安息。
「耶和华－我们的义」。
「他的名必称为『耶和华－我们的义』。」这名字惊人:它把神的名与「我们的义」连在一起。这位君王所赐的义，不是人自己挣来的，而是从神而来、白白归给「我们」的。他自己，就是我们得以站立在神面前的义。
我们的义就是基督。
这应许在基督里成就:他成了「神所立的……我们的……公义」（林前一30）。我们在神面前的义，不是自己的成绩，而是这位君王的名——「耶和华－我们的义」。信靠他的人,穿的是他的义,得的是他的救。
默想。
你在神面前的「义」，此刻建立在什么上面——自己的表现，还是基督的名？这节应许把义的重心彻底移出你之外，放在那位君王身上：「耶和华－我们的义」。今天，你能否停止靠自己挣义,单单以他的义为你站立的根据？
beats_en: A promise after failed kings.

Jeremiah had just denounced the bad shepherds "who scattered the flock" (Judah's derelict kings across generations), and immediately God promises to personally raise up a "righteous Branch" — the true Son of David. In the darkness of a declining dynasty, God lights the hope of the Messiah.
"Judah will be saved."

"In his days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely." Derelict kings only brought division and captivity; when this righteous King comes, he brings salvation and security. A true king is measured not by power, but by whether he can bring salvation, rest, to his people.
"The LORD is our righteousness."

"This is the name by which he will be called: The LORD is our righteousness." This name is astonishing: it connects God's name with "our righteousness." The righteousness this King gives is not earned by man himself, but comes from God, freely credited to "us." He himself is the righteousness by which we can stand before God.
Our righteousness is Christ.

This promise is fulfilled in Christ: he became "our righteousness" that was appointed by God (1 Corinthians 1:30). Our righteousness before God is not our own achievement, but the name of this King — "the LORD is our righteousness." Those who trust in him wear his righteousness, receive his salvation.
Meditation.

What is your "righteousness" before God built on right now — your own performance, or Christ's name? This verse moves the weight of righteousness entirely off of you, onto this King: "the LORD is our righteousness." Today, can you stop striving to earn righteousness yourself, and rely solely on his righteousness as your basis for standing?

耶利米书 29:11.verse_text: 耶和华说：我知道我向你们所怀的意念是赐平安的意念，不是降灾祸的意念，要叫你们末后有指望。
beats: 写给被掳者的信。
这节常被单独摘出励志，其实它有一个沉重的处境:耶利米写信给被掳到巴比伦的犹大人。他们的国破了、家散了，还要在异邦寄居七十年。正是对着这群前途尽毁的人，神说出「我知道我向你们所怀的意念」。
「赐平安的意念」。
「是赐平安的意念，不是降灾祸的意念。」在百姓眼中,被掳分明是灾祸;神却说,在这一切背后,他所怀的是「平安」（shalom——完整、兴盛、与神和好）的意念。神的心意,常常藏在人看似灾祸的境遇之下。
「末后有指望」。
「要叫你们末后有指望。」神没有应许立刻脱离苦境——七十年仍要熬过;他应许的是一个有盼望的结局。神的美意不总是除去苦难,而是保证苦难不是终点——「末后」有他所定的指望在等着。
指望的确据。
这份「末后的指望」在基督里得着终极的保证:神既连自己的儿子都赐给我们,「岂不也把万物和他一同白白地赐给我们吗」（罗八32）?即使身处「被掳」般的境遇,信靠他的人可以确信——他所怀的,是赐平安、给指望的意念。
默想。
你此刻是否正身处某种「被掳」——一段看不到尽头、无法自己脱离的艰难?这节不是廉价的安慰,而是对受苦之人的应许:神向你所怀的是平安、是指望,即便当下还要熬。今天,你能否相信,眼前的灾祸不是他对你的最终心意?
beats_en: A letter to the exiles.

This verse is often quoted alone for inspiration, but it actually has a heavy context: Jeremiah wrote this letter to the Judeans exiled to Babylon. Their nation was broken, families scattered, and they had to live as sojourners in a foreign land for seventy years. It was exactly to this group of people, whose future seemed utterly ruined, that God said "I know the plans I have for you."
"Plans for welfare."

"Plans for welfare and not for evil." In the people's eyes, being exiled was plainly disaster; but God says that behind all of this, what he held was "welfare" (shalom — wholeness, prosperity, reconciliation with God). God's intent is often hidden beneath what looks, to man, like disaster.
"A future and a hope."

"To give you a future and a hope." God did not promise immediate escape from hardship — the seventy years still had to be endured; what he promised was a hopeful ending. God's good will does not always remove suffering, but guarantees that suffering is not the final word — a "future" with a hope he has appointed is waiting.
The assurance of hope.

This "future hope" finds its ultimate guarantee in Christ: since God did not spare even his own Son for us, "will he not also with him graciously give us all things?" (Romans 8:32) Even amid circumstances like "exile," those who trust him can be certain — what he holds for them is a plan of welfare, of hope.
Meditation.

Are you right now in some kind of "exile" — a hardship with no end in sight, that you cannot escape on your own? This verse is not cheap comfort, but a promise to the suffering: what God holds for you is welfare, is hope, even though you still have to endure right now. Today, can you believe that the disaster in front of you is not his final intent for you?

耶利米书 31:31-33.verse_text: 耶和华说：「日子将到，我要与 以色列 家和 犹大 家另立新约，不像我拉着他们祖宗的手，领他们出 埃及 地的时候，与他们所立的约。我虽作他们的丈夫，他们却背了我的约。这是耶和华说的。」耶和华说：「那些日子以后，我与 以色列 家所立的约乃是这样：我要将我的律法放在他们里面，写在他们心上。我要作他们的 神，他们要作我的子民。
beats: 旧约中的新约。
在满纸审判的耶利米书中，这几节是最明亮的高峰:神应许要立「新约」。旧的约,百姓一次次背弃、无力遵守;神不废弃立约的心意,反而应许一个全新的、更美的约。这是整本旧约指向福音最清晰的路标之一。
旧约为何失败。
「他们却背了我的约。」旧约刻在石版上,是外在的要求;人有律法,却没有遵行的心,于是一再背约。问题从来不在律法不好,而在人的心坏了。外在的规条,改变不了里面的悖逆。
律法写在心上。
新约的关键在此:「我要将我的律法放在他们里面,写在他们心上。」不再是外面的石版,而是里面被更新的心。神不只给人当行的标准,更亲自赐下遵行的心——这是从里到外的改变,是唯有神能做的重造。
新约立在基督的血上。
主耶稣在最后晚餐举杯说:「这杯是用我血所立的新约」（路二十二20）。耶利米所预言的新约,正立在基督的宝血上:他赦免我们的罪,又赐下圣灵,把神的律法写在我们心里。我们今天所领受的,就是这新约的恩典。
默想。
你与神的关系,是停在「外在的规条」——努力遵守、屡屡失败、心里其实不情愿,还是那从里面被更新的「新约」生命?神的应许是把律法写在你心上,叫你从心里乐意亲近他。今天,你是在靠自己守规条,还是靠圣灵活出新约的生命?
beats_en: A new covenant within the old.

In a book full of judgment, these verses are the brightest peak: God promises to establish a "new covenant." The old covenant, the people broke again and again, unable to keep; God does not abandon his intent to covenant, but instead promises an entirely new, better covenant. This is one of the clearest signposts in the whole Old Testament pointing to the gospel.
Why the old covenant failed.

"They broke my covenant." The old covenant was carved on stone tablets, an outward requirement; people had the law, but no heart to keep it, and so broke covenant again and again. The problem was never that the law was bad, but that man's heart was broken. Outward rules cannot change inward rebellion.
The law written on the heart.

Here is the key of the new covenant: "I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts." No longer an outward stone tablet, but an inwardly renewed heart. God does not merely give man a standard to follow, but personally gives the heart to keep it — this is a change from inside out, a remaking only God can do.
The new covenant established on Christ's blood.

The Lord Jesus, at the Last Supper, raised the cup and said: "this cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20). The new covenant Jeremiah prophesied is exactly established on Christ's precious blood: he forgives our sins, and gives the Spirit, writing God's law on our hearts. What we receive today is the grace of this new covenant.
Meditation.

Is your relationship with God stuck at "outward rules" — trying hard, failing repeatedly, secretly unwilling — or is it that inwardly renewed "new covenant" life? God's promise is to write the law on your heart, so that you willingly draw near to him from within. Today, are you relying on yourself to keep the rules, or relying on the Spirit to live out the new covenant life?

耶利米书 36:23.verse_text: 犹底 念了三四篇 ， 王 就用文士的刀将书卷割破，扔在火盆中，直到全卷在火中烧尽了。
beats: 被焚烧的神言。
神吩咐耶利米把一切预言写在书卷上,盼望百姓听见后回转。书卷被念给约雅敬王听,王的反应却触目惊心:每念三四段,他就用文士的刀割下、扔进火盆,直到整卷烧尽。人对神话语的敌意,竟到了这个地步。
刀与火的抗拒。
「王就用文士的刀将书卷割破,扔在火盆中。」这是一幅刻意、冷静的抗拒图画——不是一时冲动,而是一段一段地割、一片一片地烧。人心对神话语的拒绝,有时不是激烈的辩驳,而是这样从容地把它一点点毁掉、拒之门外。
烧不尽的话语。
然而火烧得尽书卷,烧不尽神的话。神随即吩咐耶利米「再取一卷」,把烧掉的话重写,还加添了更多（36:32）。人可以焚烧、删改、封杀神的话,却无法废掉它——「草必枯干,花必凋残,惟有主的道是永存的」（彼前一25）。
永存的道。
约雅敬烧毁的,是一卷可以重写的书;但那永活的道成了肉身,「天地要废去,我的话却不能废去」（太二十四35）。人的抗拒改变不了神话语的结局;割破书卷的王早已灰飞烟灭,他所烧的话却存到今日,仍在审判、也在拯救人。
默想。
你未必会拿刀割神的话,但有没有某些经文,是你听了不喜欢、就悄悄「跳过」、从心里割掉的?约雅敬的从容抗拒,提醒我们省察自己对待神话语的态度。今天,神的话里有哪一句是你一直在回避、不肯让它进到心里的?
beats_en: God's word burned to ashes.

God commanded Jeremiah to write all his prophecies onto a scroll, hoping the people would turn back after hearing it. The scroll was read aloud to King Jehoiakim, and the king's reaction was jarring: every time three or four columns were read, he cut them off with a scribe's knife and threw them into the fire pot, until the whole scroll was burned. Human hostility toward God's word had reached this extent.
Resistance with knife and fire.

"The king cut it with a knife and cast it into the fire." This is a deliberate, calm picture of resistance — not a momentary impulse, but section by section cut, piece by piece burned. The heart's rejection of God's word is sometimes not fierce argument, but this calm, gradual destruction, shutting it out.
Words that cannot be burned up.

Yet though the fire could burn up the scroll, it could not burn up God's word. God immediately commanded Jeremiah to "take another scroll," rewriting the burned words, and adding even more (36:32). Man can burn, edit, suppress God's word, but cannot abolish it — "the grass withers, and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever" (1 Peter 1:25).
The eternal Word.

What Jehoiakim burned was a scroll that could be rewritten; but that eternally living Word became flesh — "heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away" (Matthew 24:35). Human resistance cannot change the outcome of God's word; the king who cut the scroll has long since turned to dust, but the word he burned remains to this day, still judging, still saving people.
Meditation.

You may not take a knife to God's word, but is there some passage you quietly "skip over" because you don't like hearing it, cutting it out of your heart? Jehoiakim's calm resistance reminds us to examine our own attitude toward God's word. Today, which line of God's word have you been avoiding, unwilling to let it into your heart?

耶利米书 45:5.verse_text: 你为自己图谋大事吗？不要图谋！我必使灾祸临到凡有血气的。但你无论往哪里去，我必使你以自己的命为掠物。这是耶和华说的。」
beats: 给灰心助手的话。
这短短一章,是神藉耶利米对他忠心的助手巴录说的。巴录抄写神的话、与先知同担逼迫,身心俱疲,发出叹息:「我有祸了!耶和华将忧愁加在我的痛苦上。」神没有责备他的软弱,却直指他心底一个隐藏的东西。
「不要图谋大事」。
「你为自己图谋大事吗?不要图谋!」神一语道破巴录疲惫背后的暗流:他心里其实还盼着自己有一番大作为、大名声。在举国将倾的时代,神提醒他放下这份「为自己」的野心——环境如此,还想成就个人的大事,只会加倍失望。
降卑时代的心态。
神要巴录看清所处的时代:「我必使灾祸临到凡有血气的。」当神正在拆毁、审判整个国家,这不是个人追求功名的时候。属灵的成熟,part是懂得在神降卑的季节里放下自我的宏图,与神的作为对齐。
以性命为掠物的恩典。
神的应许朴素却宝贵:「你无论往哪里去,我必使你以自己的命为掠物。」在众人灭亡之中,巴录能保全性命,就是极大的恩典。这预示福音的价值观:「凡为我丧掉生命的,必得着生命」（太十六25）——放下自己的大事,却在基督里保全了真正要紧的。
默想。
在你的疲惫、灰心背后,是否也藏着一个「为自己图谋大事」的落空?神对巴录的话未必是要你没有志向,而是校正那份「为自己」的野心。今天,在神所安排的这个季节里,你能否放下个人的宏图,单单忠心地站在他要你站的位置上?
beats_en: Words for a discouraged assistant.

This short chapter is God's word, through Jeremiah, to his faithful assistant Baruch. Baruch, who copied down God's word and shared in the prophet's persecution, exhausted in body and spirit, sighed: "woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain." God did not rebuke his weakness, but pointed directly to something hidden in his heart.
"Do not seek great things."

"Do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not!" God pinpoints in one sentence the undercurrent behind Baruch's exhaustion: in his heart, he still hoped for some great achievement, some great name for himself. In an age when the whole nation was collapsing, God reminds him to lay down this ambition "for himself" — with circumstances as they were, still wanting to accomplish personal greatness would only bring double disappointment.
The right mindset for a season of humbling.

God wants Baruch to see clearly the age he's in: "I am bringing disaster upon all flesh." While God is tearing down, judging the entire nation, this is not the time for personal pursuit of fame. Spiritual maturity is, in part, knowing how to lay down one's own grand ambitions in a season when God is humbling, and align with what God is doing.
The grace of life as a prize of war.

God's promise is plain yet precious: "wherever you go I will give you your life as a prize of war." Amid everyone else's destruction, Baruch being able to preserve his life is itself tremendous grace. This foretells the gospel's values: "whoever loses his life for my sake will find it" (Matthew 16:25) — laying down his own great ambition, yet in Christ preserving what truly mattered.
Meditation.

Behind your exhaustion, your discouragement, is there also hidden an unfulfilled ambition to "seek great things for yourself"? God's word to Baruch is not necessarily meant to strip you of ambition, but to correct that "for myself" motivation. Today, in this season God has arranged, can you lay down your own grand ambitions, and simply stand faithfully where he wants you to stand?

耶利米书 46:28.verse_text: 我的仆人 雅各 啊，不要惧怕！ 因我与你同在。 我要将我所赶你到的那些国灭绝净尽， 却不将你灭绝净尽， 倒要从宽惩治你， 万不能不罚你 。 这是耶和华说的。
beats: 列国审判中的安慰。
耶利米书末段是对列国的审判预言,一片刀剑与倾覆之声。就在对埃及的审判之后,神忽然转向他的百姓雅各,说出一句温柔的安慰。审判的雷声之中,神没有忘记他立约的子民——他的管教与他的信实,从不分家。
「因我与你同在」。
「不要惧怕!因我与你同在。」神驱散惧怕的方式,不是保证一路顺遂,而是保证他的同在。列国要被灭绝净尽,雅各却有神与他同在——这才是他与列国命运不同的根本原因。有神同在,就有不惧怕的底气。
管教却不灭绝。
「我要将……那些国灭绝净尽,却不将你灭绝净尽,倒要从宽惩治你,万不能不罚你。」神对自己儿女的对待,与对列国截然不同:列国是被灭绝,儿女是被管教。他「万不能不罚」——因他爱得认真;却「不灭绝」——因他守约到底。
管教是爱的记号。
这「惩治却不灭绝」的分别,新约说得明白:「主所爱的,他必管教……你们所忍受的,是神管教你们,待你们如同待儿子」（来十二6-7）。神的管教不是要毁掉我们,而是爱的记号——证明我们是他不肯放弃的儿女。
默想。
当神的管教临到,你是否把它误当作他的弃绝、心生惧怕?这节经文分辨了两件事:列国被灭绝,儿女被管教。今天你所经历的难处,若是神的管教,那恰恰证明你是他所爱、「万不能不罚」却「绝不灭绝」的儿女——他与你同在。
beats_en: Comfort amid the judgment of the nations.

The latter section of Jeremiah is prophecy of judgment against the nations, full of the sound of swords and overthrow. Right after the judgment on Egypt, God suddenly turns to his own people Jacob, speaking a tender word of comfort. Amid the thunder of judgment, God has not forgotten his covenant people — his discipline and his faithfulness are never separated.
"For I am with you."

"Fear not... for I am with you." God's way of dispelling fear is not guaranteeing smooth sailing all the way, but guaranteeing his presence. The nations would be utterly destroyed, but Jacob has God with him — this is the fundamental reason his fate differs from the nations'. With God present, there is confidence to be unafraid.
Disciplined, yet not destroyed.

"I will make a full end of... those nations... but of you I will not make a full end. I will discipline you in just measure, and I will by no means leave you unpunished." God's treatment of his own children is entirely different from his treatment of the nations: the nations are destroyed, the children are disciplined. He "will by no means leave unpunished" — because he loves seriously; yet "will not make a full end" — because he keeps covenant to the end.
Discipline is the mark of love.

This distinction of "disciplined but not destroyed" is stated plainly in the New Testament: "the Lord disciplines the one he loves... it is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons" (Hebrews 12:6-7). God's discipline is not meant to destroy us, but is the mark of love — proof that we are children he refuses to give up on.
Meditation.

When God's discipline comes, do you mistake it for his rejection, growing afraid? This verse distinguishes two things: the nations are destroyed, the children are disciplined. If the difficulty you're experiencing today is God's discipline, that exactly proves you are his beloved child, whom he "will by no means leave unpunished" yet "will never destroy" — he is with you.

耶利米书 51:24.verse_text: 耶和华说：「我必在你们眼前报复 巴比伦 人和 迦勒底 居民在 锡安 所行的诸恶。」
beats: 向巴比伦讨还。
耶利米书以对巴比伦的长篇审判作结。这个曾被神用作管教以色列之杖的强国,如今轮到它受审。神宣告:「我必在你们眼前报复巴比伦人……在锡安所行的诸恶。」神使用列国施行管教,不等于纵容它们的残暴。
「在锡安所行的诸恶」。
巴比伦毁圣殿、掳百姓、极尽羞辱,以为自己战无不胜。神却记下它「在锡安所行的诸恶」,一笔一笔都要追讨。作恶者若以为神不看、不算,那是大错——神看见,神记念,神必在他所定的日子报应。
「在你们眼前」的公义。
「我必在你们眼前报复」——神的伸冤不是暗中进行,而是要公开彰显,叫受欺压的百姓亲眼看见公义。受苦的义人不必自己报复,也不必怀疑神是否公义;神必在众人眼前,把该讨的讨回来。
伸冤在主。
巴比伦的结局,印证了神的话:「伸冤在我,我必报应」（罗十二19）。信徒因此可以不必以恶报恶,而把冤情交给那位公义的审判者。这份公义在十字架上更显奇妙:神既在基督身上刑罚了罪,又给悔改的仇敌留下回转之路。
默想。
当你被人欺压、亏待,却无处申冤时,心里是想亲自报复,还是能把冤情交给那位「必在众人眼前报复」的神?巴比伦的下场提醒你:神都看见、都记念、都必追讨。今天,有没有一桩你紧抓不放的冤屈,可以交在他公义的手中?
beats_en: A reckoning with Babylon.

Jeremiah closes with a lengthy judgment against Babylon. This powerful nation, once used by God as a rod to discipline Israel, now takes its turn to be judged. God declares: "I will repay Babylon and all the inhabitants of Chaldea for all the evil that they have done in Zion." God using the nations to carry out discipline does not mean condoning their cruelty.
"All the evil done in Zion."

Babylon destroyed the temple, carried off the people, humiliated them to the utmost, thinking itself invincible. But God records "all the evil done in Zion," every single item to be reckoned. If evildoers think God doesn't see, doesn't count, that is a grave mistake — God sees, God remembers, God will surely repay on his appointed day.
Justice 'before your eyes.'

"I will repay before your eyes" — God's vindication is not carried out secretly, but publicly displayed, so the oppressed people see justice with their own eyes. The suffering righteous need not avenge themselves, nor doubt whether God is just; God will surely, before everyone's eyes, repay what needs repaying.
Vengeance belongs to the Lord.

Babylon's fate confirms God's word: "vengeance is mine, I will repay" (Romans 12:19). Believers can therefore avoid repaying evil with evil, handing their grievance over to that righteous Judge instead. This justice is even more wondrously displayed on the cross: God both punished sin in Christ, and left a road of return for repentant enemies.
Meditation.

When you're oppressed, wronged, with nowhere to plead your case, does your heart want to avenge itself, or can you hand the grievance over to the God who "will surely repay before everyone's eyes"? Babylon's fate reminds you: God sees it all, remembers it all, will surely call it to account. Today, is there a grievance you've been gripping tightly, that you could hand over to his righteous hand?

耶利米哀歌 3:22-23.verse_text: 我们不致消灭， 是出于耶和华诸般的慈爱； 是因他的怜悯不致断绝。每早晨，这都是新的； 你的诚实极其广大！
beats: 废墟中的转折。
耶利米哀歌是为耶路撒冷的毁灭而写的挽歌,字字是灰烬与眼泪。全卷五章的正中央——第三章的正中间——却陡然亮起一道光。就在最深的哀痛里,诗人抓住一个不肯放手的确据,唱出全卷、也是圣经中最动人的信实之歌。
「不致消灭」的缘由。
「我们不致消灭,是出于耶和华诸般的慈爱;是因他的怜悯不致断绝。」城虽毁、民虽亡,却「不致消灭」——余种仍存。诗人看清:他们还活着,不是因自己still有什么,而全然是神的慈爱与怜悯没有断绝。
「每早晨都是新的」。
「每早晨,这都是新的;你的诚实极其广大!」神的怜悯不是有限的库存,用一点少一点;而是每个清晨都重新涌流、取之不尽。昨天的失败与眼泪,挡不住今晨新赐的怜悯。神的信实,像日出一样按时、可靠、崭新。
永不断绝的信实。
这份「每早晨都是新的」慈爱,在基督里成了确据:「他既然爱世间属自己的人,就爱他们到底」（约十三1）。神的怜悯之所以「不致断绝」,是因它立在基督永远的救赎上——即使在人生的废墟里,这怜悯每早晨仍然如新地临到。
默想。
你是否正站在某种「废墟」里——被过去的失败、眼泪或损失压得抬不起头?哀歌的诗人在灰烬中仍能说「他的怜悯不致断绝,每早晨都是新的」。今天是新的一天,神的怜悯又一次为你重新涌流。你能否抓住这份每晨如新的信实,重新站起?
beats_en: A turning point amid the ruins.

Lamentations is a dirge written for the destruction of Jerusalem, every word ash and tears. Right at the very center of the whole five chapters — the exact middle of chapter 3 — a light suddenly breaks through. Right in the deepest grief, the poet holds onto one certainty he won't let go of, singing the whole book's, and perhaps Scripture's, most moving song of faithfulness.
The reason 'we are not consumed.'

"The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end." Though the city was destroyed and the people perished, they "are not consumed" — a remnant remained. The poet saw clearly: that they were still alive was not because of anything they still had, but entirely because God's steadfast love and mercy had not ceased.
"New every morning."

"They are new every morning; great is your faithfulness!" God's mercy is not a limited stock, dwindling with use, but flows afresh every morning, inexhaustible. Yesterday's failures and tears cannot block this morning's newly given mercy. God's faithfulness, like the sunrise, is punctual, reliable, ever new.
Faithfulness that never ceases.

This "new every morning" steadfast love became certainty in Christ: "having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end" (John 13:1). God's mercy "never ceases" precisely because it is founded on Christ's eternal redemption — even amid life's ruins, this mercy still arrives fresh, every morning.
Meditation.

Are you standing right now in some kind of "ruins" — weighed down, unable to lift your head, by past failures, tears, or losses? The poet of Lamentations, even amid the ashes, could still say "his mercies never come to an end, they are new every morning." Today is a new day, and God's mercy flows afresh for you once more. Can you grasp this ever-new-every-morning faithfulness, and stand up again?

以西结书 3:17.verse_text: 「人子啊，我立你作 以色列 家守望的人，所以你要听我口中的话，替我警戒他们。
beats: 守望者的托付。
以西结蒙召之初,神就给他一个沉甸甸的身份:「我立你作以色列家守望的人。」守望者站在城墙上,一见刀剑临近就吹角警告全城。神把先知的职分,定义为这样一个警戒的岗位——不为讨人喜欢,只为忠实地传递警报。
「听我口中的话」。
守望者首先要做的,是「听我口中的话」。他不能吹自己的号、传自己的想法,只能忠实转达神所说的。忠心事奉的核心,从来不是有多少创意或口才,而是先安静聆听神,再准确地把神的话传出去。
「替我警戒他们」。
「替我警戒他们。」守望者的责任是发出警告;至于人听不听,不在他掌控。接下来神说,守望者若不警戒,罪人的血要归到他手里;若警戒了,人不听,他就尽了本分。忠心的标准,是有没有把该说的说出来,而非结果如何。
为羊舍命的守望者。
以西结是站在城墙上示警的守望者;而主耶稣是那位「好牧人」,不只警告羊群,更亲自「为羊舍命」（约十11）。他既是发声的守望者,又是替我们承担刑罚的救主——他警戒我们逃避将来的忿怒,又亲自为我们担当了那忿怒。
默想。
神也把身边一些人「托付」给了你——家人、朋友、同事。作为一个属灵的守望者,你是否忠实地把神的真理、必要的提醒传给他们,还是因怕得罪人而选择沉默?今天,有没有一句该说的真话,是你出于爱、也出于忠心,该向某人说出的?
beats_en: The watchman's charge.

At the very start of his calling, God gave Ezekiel a weighty identity: "I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel." A watchman stands on the city wall, and the moment he sees the sword approaching, sounds the trumpet to warn the whole city. God defines the prophet's office as exactly this kind of watchful post — not to please people, but to faithfully relay the alarm.
"Hear the word from my mouth."

The watchman's first task is to "hear the word from my mouth." He cannot sound his own trumpet, spread his own thoughts, only faithfully relay what God has said. The core of faithful service has never been how much creativity or eloquence one has, but first quietly listening to God, then accurately delivering God's word.
"Give them warning from me."

"Give them warning from me." The watchman's responsibility is to sound the warning; whether people listen or not is beyond his control. God then says, if the watchman fails to warn, the sinner's blood is on his hands; if he warns and they don't listen, he has fulfilled his duty. The standard of faithfulness is whether he said what needed saying, not the outcome.
The watchman who laid down his life for the sheep.

Ezekiel is a watchman standing on the wall sounding the alarm; the Lord Jesus is that "good shepherd," who not only warns the flock, but personally "lays down his life for the sheep" (John 10:11). He is both the sounding watchman, and the Savior who bears the punishment in our place — he warns us to flee the coming wrath, and personally bore that wrath for us.
Meditation.

God has also "entrusted" some people around you to you — family, friends, coworkers. As a spiritual watchman, are you faithfully delivering God's truth, the necessary warnings, to them, or choosing silence out of fear of offending? Today, is there a true word that needs saying, that, out of love and out of faithfulness, you should speak to someone?

以西结书 7:3.verse_text: 现在你的结局已经临到，我必使我的怒气归与你，也必按你的行为审判你，照你一切可憎的事刑罚你。
beats: 「结局临到了」。
以西结反复宣告一个沉重的词:「结局」。百姓以为日子还会照常过下去,神却宣告:「现在你的结局已经临到。」人最大的错觉,是以为审判永远不会来、时间永远还有;神却提醒,罪恶累积到尽头,必有一个「结局」。
「按你的行为审判」。
「必按你的行为审判你,照你一切可憎的事刑罚你。」神的审判不是任意的,而是「按行为」——公正、对应、毫不冤枉。他们种下的可憎之事,如今要照样收成。神看得清清楚楚,量得公公道道。
罪的必然后果。
本章反复出现「结局」「日子近了」,是要打破一种致命的麻木:以为可以一直犯罪而不必付代价。神的怒气不是情绪的爆发,而是他圣洁对罪必然的回应。轻看罪、拖延悔改的人,终究要面对那必来的结局。
承担结局的主。
神「按行为审判」是绝对公义的;而福音的惊人之处,是基督替我们承担了本该临到我们的「结局」。他在十字架上受了我们「可憎之事」当受的刑罚,好叫信他的人,那已定的审判「结局」,变成永生的开始（约五24）。
默想。
你是否也活在一种「还早着呢」的属灵麻木里,把悔改一拖再拖,仿佛结局永远不会来?以西结的警告是:结局必临到,审判按行为。今天,有没有一件你一直拖延不肯对付的罪?趁着还有「今天」,回到那位替你担了结局的主面前。
beats_en: "The end has come."

Ezekiel repeatedly declares a heavy word: "the end." The people thought life would go on as usual, but God declares: "now the end is upon you." Man's greatest illusion is thinking judgment will never come, that there's always more time; but God reminds them, when sin accumulates to its full measure, an "end" will surely come.
"Judge you according to your ways."

"I will judge you according to your ways, and will punish you for all your abominations." God's judgment is not arbitrary, but "according to ways" — fair, corresponding, wronging no one. What they sowed in abomination, they will now reap in kind. God sees everything clearly, and weighs everything justly.
The inevitable consequence of sin.

"The end," "the day is near" recurs throughout this chapter, meant to break a fatal numbness: thinking one can keep sinning forever without cost. God's anger is not an emotional outburst, but his holiness's inevitable response to sin. Those who take sin lightly, delaying repentance, will eventually have to face that certain end.
The Lord who bore the end.

God "judging according to ways" is absolutely just; and the astonishing thing about the gospel is that Christ bore, in our place, the "end" that should have come upon us. He bore, on the cross, the punishment our "abominations" deserved, so that for those who believe in him, that fixed judgment's "end" becomes the beginning of eternal life (John 5:24).
Meditation.

Are you also living in a kind of spiritual numbness of "there's still plenty of time," putting off repentance again and again, as if the end will never come? Ezekiel's warning is: the end will surely come, judgment according to deeds. Today, is there a sin you've been putting off, unwilling to deal with? While there is still "today," return before this Lord who bore the end for you.

以西结书 11:19.verse_text: 我要使他们有合一的心，也要将新灵放在他们里面，又从他们肉体中除掉石心，赐给他们肉心，
beats: 审判中的应许。
以西结书前段满是审判,但这一节像黑夜里的一线曙光。神看清了以色列的病根不在外面,而在里面——那颗刚硬、悖逆、无力顺服的心。于是他应许要做一件唯有他能做的事:动手术,换一颗心。
除掉石心。
「从他们肉体中除掉石心。」「石心」是一颗对神冷硬、无感、拒绝的心。人靠自己无法软化它——石头不能自己变肉。以西结指出人最深的问题:不是行为不够好,而是心已经硬如顽石,需要被神亲手取出。
赐给肉心。
「赐给他们肉心。」神不只除去旧的,更换上新的——一颗柔软、有感觉、肯回应神的心。「合一的心」「新灵」都在其中:这是一场从里到外的更新,不是修补,而是重造。人能有的最大转变,是神换给他一颗新心。
新心的成就。
这换心的应许,唯在新约里、藉圣灵成就:「若有人在基督里,他就是新造的人」（林后五17）。信主不只是行为的改良,而是神真的取走石心、赐下肉心、把他的灵放在我们里面。我们能爱神、肯顺服,本身就是这应许在我们身上的果子。
默想。
你是否在某个领域感到自己的心「硬如石头」——对神的话无动于衷、对某个人无法饶恕、对该悔改的事毫无感觉?好消息是:软化石心不是靠你咬牙努力,而是神应许要亲自更换。今天,你能否求他在那一处,除掉你的石心,赐你一颗肉心?
beats_en: A promise amid judgment.

The early part of Ezekiel is full of judgment, but this verse is like a ray of dawn light in the night. God saw clearly that Israel's disease was not outward, but inward — that hardened, rebellious, disobedient heart. So he promises to do something only he can do: perform surgery, exchange the heart.
Removing the heart of stone.

"I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh." A "heart of stone" is a heart cold, unfeeling, resistant toward God. Man cannot soften it himself — a stone cannot turn itself to flesh. Ezekiel points out humanity's deepest problem: not that behavior isn't good enough, but that the heart has already hardened like a stubborn stone, needing to be removed by God's own hand.
Giving a heart of flesh.

"And give them a heart of flesh." God does not merely remove the old — he replaces it with the new: a soft, feeling heart, willing to respond to God. "A heart of one accord," "a new spirit" are all included: this is a renewal from inside out, not a patch, but a remaking. The greatest transformation a person can undergo is God exchanging their heart for a new one.
The fulfillment of the new heart.

This promise of an exchanged heart is fulfilled only in the New Testament, through the Spirit: "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation" (2 Corinthians 5:17). Believing in the Lord is not merely behavioral improvement, but God truly taking away the heart of stone, giving a heart of flesh, and placing his Spirit within us. Our ability to love God, to be willing to obey, is itself the fruit of this promise in us.
Meditation.

Is there some area where you feel your own heart "hard as stone" — indifferent to God's word, unable to forgive someone, feeling nothing about something you should repent of? The good news is: softening a heart of stone does not depend on your gritted-teeth effort, but is God's promise to personally exchange it. Today, can you ask him, in that place, to remove your heart of stone, and give you a heart of flesh?

以西结书 14:14.verse_text: 其中虽有 挪亚 、 但以理 、 约伯 这三人，他们只能因他们的义救自己的性命。这是主耶和华说的。
beats: 三个义人也救不了。
百姓以为城中有几个义人,神就必因他们的缘故手下留情。神却举出历史上三位公认的义人——挪亚、但以理、约伯——郑重宣告:即便他们同在城中,「也只能因他们的义救自己的性命」,救不了别人。审判临头,借不来别人的义。
义不能转借。
挪亚在洪水中蒙拯救,但以理在被掳中蒙保守,约伯在苦难中被称义——都是响当当的义人。然而神说,他们的义只够救自己。这戳破一个幻想:以为可以靠祖先的敬虔、旁人的属灵来庇荫自己。在神面前,每个人都要为自己负责。
个人的责任。
以西结书反复强调个人在神面前的责任(参18章)。没有人能踩着别人的信仰进天国,也没有人能被别人的罪连累而失丧。这既是严肃的警告——你无法躲在别人的义后面;也是公平的保证——神照各人自己的光景审判。
唯一能救众人的义。
挪亚、但以理、约伯的义都只够救自己;但有一位的义,却足以救众人——基督。他是唯一「义能转借」的那一位:他把自己的义归给一切信他的人,「因一人的顺从,众人也成为义了」（罗五19）。人无法靠别人的义得救,却能靠他的义得救。
默想。
你是否暗暗靠着「家里有人信主」「教会里属灵人多」来安慰自己,却迟迟不亲自面对神?这段经文提醒:别人的义救不了你。但也有大好的消息:有一位的义足以救你——基督。今天,你的得救,是靠旁人的信,还是你自己与他之间真实的信靠?
beats_en: Even three righteous men could not save others.

The people thought that if there were a few righteous people in the city, God would surely spare it for their sake. But God names three historically acknowledged righteous men — Noah, Daniel, Job — and solemnly declares: even if they were all in the city together, "they would deliver but their own lives by their righteousness." They could not save others. When judgment comes, another's righteousness cannot be borrowed.
Righteousness cannot be transferred.

Noah was saved in the flood, Daniel was preserved in exile, Job was declared righteous in suffering — all unmistakably righteous men. Yet God says their righteousness was only enough to save themselves. This punctures an illusion: that one can shelter under an ancestor's devotion, or another's spirituality. Before God, everyone is responsible for themselves.
Individual responsibility.

Ezekiel repeatedly emphasizes individual responsibility before God (see chapter 18). No one can enter heaven riding on another's faith, and no one is lost through another's sin. This is both a solemn warning — you cannot hide behind someone else's righteousness — and a fair assurance — God judges each according to their own condition.
The one righteousness that can save everyone.

The righteousness of Noah, Daniel, and Job was only enough to save themselves; but there is one whose righteousness is enough to save everyone — Christ. He is the only one whose righteousness "can be transferred": he credits his own righteousness to all who believe in him — "by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous" (Romans 5:19). Man cannot be saved by another's righteousness, but can be saved by his.
Meditation.

Are you secretly comforting yourself with "someone in my family believes" or "there are many spiritual people in the church," while continuing to delay facing God yourself? This passage reminds you: another's righteousness cannot save you. But there is great news: one's righteousness is enough to save you — Christ's. Today, is your salvation relying on someone else's faith, or on real trust between you and him?

以西结书 18:32.verse_text: 主耶和华说：我不喜悦那死人之死，所以你们当回头而存活。」
beats: 审判者的心肠。
以西结十八章反复申明:犯罪的必死,回转的必活,各人担自己的罪。就在这严厉的审判逻辑之后,神袒露了他的心:「我不喜悦那死人之死。」神宣告审判,却不以罪人的灭亡为乐——这是审判话语背后,那颗不忍的父心。
「不喜悦人死亡」。
「我不喜悦那死人之死。」神有权、也必按公义审判罪;但他心里真正的渴望,不是定罪,而是人回转得生。审判是他不得不行的公义,拯救才是他心中所喜悦的。这一句,让我们看见公义背后那深切的爱。
「回头而存活」。
「所以你们当回头而存活。」神发出的不是绝望的判决,而是恳切的邀请:回头,就能存活!悔改的路一直敞开着。神摆在人面前的,从来不是「反正都要死」,而是「你们回头吧,好叫你们活」。存活的门,是他亲手为悔改者留的。
寻找罪人的主。
这位「不喜悦人死亡、愿人回转」的神,在基督里亲自来寻找失丧的人。主耶稣说他来「是要寻找拯救失丧的人」（路十九10）,又用浪子的父亲、寻羊的牧人,把神「不愿一人沉沦,乃愿人人悔改」（彼后三9）的心肠,画得淋漓尽致。
默想。
你心里的神,是一位巴不得抓人错处、乐于定罪的神,还是这位「不喜悦人死亡、恳切呼人回头存活」的神?这节校正我们对神的看法。今天,若你正因某个罪而不敢回转、以为神已厌弃你,请听他真实的心声:「回头吧,好叫你存活。」
beats_en: The judge's heart.

Ezekiel 18 repeatedly states: whoever sins will die, whoever turns will live, each bears their own sin. Right after this stern logic of judgment, God bares his heart: "I have no pleasure in the death of anyone." God declares judgment, yet does not delight in the sinner's destruction — this is the compassionate father's heart behind the words of judgment.
"Not delighting in death."

"I have no pleasure in the death of anyone." God has the right, and must, judge sin according to justice; but what his heart truly longs for is not condemnation, but that people turn and live. Judgment is the justice he cannot avoid; salvation is what his heart delights in. This one sentence lets us see the deep love behind justice.
"Turn, and live."

"So turn, and live." What God issues is not a hopeless verdict, but an earnest invitation: turn, and you can live! The road of repentance stands ever open. What God places before man is never "you're going to die anyway," but "turn, so that you may live." The door to life is one he has personally left open for the repentant.
The Lord who seeks the sinner.

This God who "takes no pleasure in death, longs for people to turn," personally comes in Christ to seek the lost. The Lord Jesus said he came "to seek and to save the lost" (Luke 19:10), and through the parables of the prodigal's father, the shepherd seeking the sheep, painted vividly God's heart of "not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance" (2 Peter 3:9).
Meditation.

Is the God in your heart one eager to catch you in the wrong, delighting to condemn, or this God who "takes no pleasure in death, earnestly calls people to turn and live"? This verse corrects our view of God. Today, if you're afraid to turn because of some sin, thinking God has already rejected you, hear his true heart's voice: "turn, so that you may live."

以西结书 24:16.verse_text: 「人子啊，我要将你眼目所喜爱的忽然取去，你却不可悲哀哭泣，也不可流泪，
beats: 先知以生命作预言。
神常叫以西结用行动来传信息;而这一次,代价大到令人屏息。神预告要「将你眼目所喜爱的忽然取去」——指他深爱的妻子。以西结要在丧妻之痛中,遵神的命不哭不泣,好成为百姓的一个「预兆」。传神话语的人,有时要用自己的生命去承载它。
「眼目所喜爱的」。
「你眼目所喜爱的」——神知道以西结的妻子在他心中的分量。神从不轻看我们所珍爱的;他明明知道那份爱有多深,才用这样的字眼。这提醒我们:神所要求于仆人的舍弃,他自己都看在眼里、都懂得那份疼。
顺服中的痛。
以西结照命而行:早晨说预言,晚上妻子就死了,次日他便遵命不举哀。这是一种在剧痛中依然完全的顺服。它不美化苦难,也不假装不痛;而是在最深的失去中,仍选择信靠、仍站在神要他站的位置上。
神也失去所爱。
以西结失去「眼目所喜爱的」,预表百姓将失去他们眼目所喜爱的圣殿。但这幅图画背后,还有更深的一层:神自己也曾「不爱惜自己的儿子,为我们众人舍了」（罗八32）。神所要求以西结承受的失去,他自己在十字架上承受得更深。
默想。
神有时会触碰甚至取走我们「眼目所喜爱的」——一个人、一样恩赐、一个梦想。在那样的失去里,你是转身埋怨,还是像以西结那样,在痛中仍选择信靠、顺服?今天,你手中有没有一样「眼目所喜爱的」,是神要你学习松开、单单以他为至宝的?
beats_en: The prophet prophesies with his own life.

God often had Ezekiel convey messages through action; this time, the cost was breathtaking. God foretold he would "take away from you the delight of your eyes" — meaning his beloved wife. Ezekiel had to, in the midst of grieving her loss, obey God's command not to weep, not to mourn, so as to become a "sign" to the people. Those who deliver God's word sometimes must carry it with their own life.
"The delight of your eyes."

"The delight of your eyes" — God knew the weight of Ezekiel's wife in his heart. God never treats what we treasure lightly; he uses this exact phrase because he knows precisely how deep that love ran. This reminds us: whatever sacrifice God requires of his servants, he himself sees it, and understands the pain.
Pain within obedience.

Ezekiel did as commanded: he prophesied in the morning, and his wife died that evening; the next day he obeyed, not mourning. This is a complete obedience that remained even amid agonizing pain. It does not glamorize suffering, nor pretend it doesn't hurt; but in the deepest loss, still chooses to trust, still stands where God wants him to stand.
God also lost his beloved.

Ezekiel losing "the delight of his eyes" foreshadows the people losing the temple, the delight of their eyes. But behind this picture lies an even deeper layer: God himself "did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all" (Romans 8:32). The loss God required Ezekiel to bear, he himself bore even more deeply on the cross.
Meditation.

God sometimes touches, even takes away, "the delight of our eyes" — a person, a gift, a dream. In that kind of loss, do you turn and complain, or, like Ezekiel, still choose to trust and obey through the pain? Today, is there something "the delight of your eyes" in your hands, that God wants you to learn to release, treasuring him alone as your greatest prize?

以西结书 28:17.verse_text: 你因美丽心中高傲， 又因荣光败坏智慧， 我已将你摔倒在地， 使你倒在君王面前， 好叫他们目睹眼见。
beats: 推罗王的堕落。
这是对推罗王的哀歌。经文的用词远超一个人间君王——「你曾在伊甸神的园中」「受膏遮掩约柜的基路伯」,许多解经者由此看见,推罗王的骄傲背后,映着那更古老的堕落者的影子。人间的自高,往往是那原初悖逆的回响。
「因美丽心中高傲」。
「你因美丽心中高傲。」推罗富甲一方、繁华夺目,王便把这一切算作自己的荣耀,心就高傲起来。神所赐的美善——才干、成就、外貌、财富——一旦被人据为自己的荣耀,就成了骄傲的温床。恩赐本是好的,居功却是致命的。
「因荣光败坏智慧」。
「又因荣光败坏智慧。」骄傲会腐蚀判断力:越自觉荣耀,越看不清真相。推罗的智慧本是它的骄傲之一,如今反被这骄傲败坏。自高之人最终会失去分辨——因为他把自己放在了神的位置上,再也看不清自己不过是受造者。
降卑与升高的对比。
「我已将你摔倒在地。」自高的结局是被摔下。这正与基督成了鲜明对比:他「本有神的形像」,却不夸耀、反倒虚己、自甘卑微,神因此「将他升为至高」（腓二6-9）。堕落者因自高而坠落,救主因降卑而被高举——这是两条相反的路。
默想。
你所拥有的美善——能力、外貌、成就——是让你更感恩、更谦卑地归荣耀给神,还是悄悄成了你「心中高傲」的资本?推罗的下场警戒我们:恩赐居功,必招败坏。今天,有哪一样神的恩赐,是你需要重新交还、把荣耀归还给赐予者的?
beats_en: The fall of the king of Tyre.

This is a dirge against the king of Tyre. The language far exceeds an earthly king — "you were in Eden, the garden of God," "an anointed guardian cherub" — many commentators see, behind the pride of the king of Tyre, the shadow of that more ancient fallen one. Human self-exaltation is often an echo of that original rebellion.
"Your heart was proud because of your beauty."

"Your heart was proud because of your beauty." Tyre was fabulously wealthy, dazzlingly prosperous, and the king counted all of this as his own glory, and his heart grew proud. The good things God gives — talent, achievement, appearance, wealth — once claimed by man as his own glory, become a breeding ground for pride. The gift is good; taking credit for it is fatal.
"Corrupted your wisdom because of your splendor."

"You corrupted your wisdom for the sake of your splendor." Pride corrodes judgment: the more self-consciously glorious, the less clearly one sees the truth. Tyre's wisdom was once its pride, and now was corrupted by that very pride instead. The self-exalted eventually lose discernment — because they've placed themselves in God's position, no longer able to see clearly that they're merely creatures.
The contrast between being brought low and being lifted up.

"I cast you to the ground." The end of self-exaltation is being thrown down. This stands in sharp contrast to Christ: "though he was in the form of God," he did not boast, but instead emptied himself, willingly humble, and God therefore "has highly exalted him" (Philippians 2:6-9). The fallen one fell because of self-exaltation; the Savior was lifted up because of humbling himself — two opposite roads.
Meditation.

The good things you possess — ability, appearance, achievement — are they leading you to be more grateful, more humbly giving glory to God, or have they quietly become your "proud heart's" capital? Tyre's fate warns us: taking credit for a gift will surely bring ruin. Today, which of God's gifts do you need to hand back over, returning the glory to the giver?

以西结书 29:3.verse_text: 说主耶和华如此说： 埃及 王法老啊， 我与你这卧在自己河中的大鱼为敌。 你曾说：这河是我的， 是我为自己造的。
beats: 对埃及的审判。
神向埃及王法老宣告审判,用了一个极生动的比喻:「我与你这卧在自己河中的大鱼为敌。」法老自比为盘踞尼罗河的巨兽,不可一世。神却宣告要与他为敌——再庞大的势力,一旦与神作对,结局都已注定。
「这河是我的」。
法老口出狂言:「这河是我的,是我为自己造的。」尼罗河是埃及的命脉与骄傲,法老竟宣称是自己造的、归自己所有。这是人骄傲的极致:把神所赐、所造的一切,据为己有,俨然以创造者自居。忘记源头的人,总会说出这样的话。
受造者的僭越。
「是我为自己造的」——这句话把受造者与造物主的界限彻底抹去。法老享受尼罗河的丰盛,却否认这一切来自神;他把管家当成了主人。这正是罪的核心:不承认「万物都从神而来」,反把功劳、主权都揽到自己身上。
承认主权的智慧。
法老说「河是我的」,尼布甲尼撒却在被降卑后学会说「天上掌权的是至高者」（但四）。这两种结局的分野,在于肯不肯承认神的主权。真智慧始于承认:我所有的一切——才干、机会、成就——都不是「我为自己造的」,而是神所赐的。
默想。
你是否也在某些事上,不知不觉说着「这是我的,是我为自己挣来的」——你的事业、财富、家庭、才干?法老的狂言提醒我们省察:我们太容易把神的恩赐当成自己的功劳。今天,有哪一样「河」,是你需要重新承认「这是神的」?
beats_en: Judgment on Egypt.

God declares judgment on Pharaoh, king of Egypt, using an extremely vivid metaphor: "behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lies in the midst of his streams." Pharaoh saw himself as the great beast dominating the Nile, unrivaled. But God declares he would oppose him — however massive a power, once it opposes God, its end is already sealed.
"This river is my own."
